messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Policy Analyst
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

Vignette:
Marianne had spent most of her career as a policy analyst in a downtown state office, a work life built around careful reading, public meetings, and long hours at a desk, and she had always considered herself methodical and steady. That sense of herself changed after the toxic chemical exposure at a small industrial site outside the city, where she had been visiting with colleagues as part of a policy review. The visit was supposed to be brief. Instead, an unexpected release of chemicals spread through the area, and in the confusion she found herself breathing an acrid, burnt odor that seemed to cling to the back of her throat. She remembered the smell of smoke and something scorched, and the fact that no one could tell her immediately what it was. Later, when the danger was over and she was physically safe, it was the memory of that smell that stayed with her most vividly, along with the sharp awareness that the air itself had seemed wrong.

In the weeks that followed, Marianne began to notice how quickly her body reacted when she encountered anything that reminded her of that day. If she passed a building with a faint burnt odor from a kitchen, or if a neighbor’s grill gave off a smell that resembled smoke, she would feel a sudden tightening in her chest and a surge of alarm before she had fully registered what she was smelling. The smell of alcohol had become similarly difficult for her; what once would have been a neutral part of everyday life could now make her feel abruptly on edge, as if some hidden danger might be near. She would stop mid-conversation, inhale sharply, and look around with a start, certain for a moment that something was wrong. These reactions could come on so strongly that she had to steady herself before she could continue what she was doing.

Marianne also became preoccupied with trying to figure out whether the event could have been prevented. She would go over the sequence again and again in her mind, replaying the decisions made before the exposure and the moments when warning signs might have been missed. She knew she was searching for a point at which someone, perhaps herself, should have done something differently. This habit of mental reviewing had become especially noticeable in the evenings, when she would sit at the kitchen table after work and turn the day over in her mind, asking herself whether she should have questioned the site conditions more carefully or insisted on leaving sooner. Even as she recognized that she could not change what happened, she found herself returning to it, as if understanding the failure might somehow make the world feel more manageable.

At the same time, she grew increasingly watchful in daily life. When she entered a conference room at work, she would scan the exits before sitting down. In restaurants, waiting areas, and even in her own church hall on Sundays, she would choose a seat based on how protected she felt, preferring a place near a door or with a clear view of the room. She said she now did this automatically, almost before she realized she had started looking. The habit had spread into routine errands as well: in offices, stores, and unfamiliar buildings, she checked where the exits were as soon as she walked in. It gave her a sense of needing to be prepared, because she did not trust that she would notice danger quickly enough if something happened again.

As weeks turned into months, Marianne began avoiding television programs, films, and articles about industrial accidents, fires, or toxic exposures. If a news segment showed smoke pouring from a building or a story mentioned chemical fumes, she would change the channel or leave the room. She disliked how quickly her body reacted and how long it took to settle afterward, and she did not want to invite more of those experiences into her day. Her husband noticed that she was less willing to watch the evening news with him, and she started reading less of the kinds of investigative reports she had once handled comfortably for work. In her office, where policy discussions sometimes touched on emergency preparedness or industrial safety, she became more guarded and hesitant. She worried that she could not rely on herself the way she used to, that she might miss something important or fail to respond properly if a similar situation arose. That self-doubt became especially painful because her work had always depended on judgment and careful decision-making.

Marianne also described a quieter, more disturbing change in the way she experienced her own emotions. She said she felt as though she would never be able to feel normal emotions again, and that even moments that should have been comforting or moving seemed muted or out of reach. She did not describe feeling detached in dramatic terms; instead, she spoke with sadness about how ordinary pleasure and ease no longer felt quite the same. That belief made her fearful in a different way, as if something essential in her had been altered and might not return.

By the time she sought help, Marianne had become tired of living with the constant vigilance, the mental replaying, and the limits she had placed on herself. She was especially troubled by how easily a smell could pull her back into that day and how much effort it took to feel settled in a room or at work. She came to therapy hoping to make sense of why the danger still felt so immediate, and fearing that if nothing changed she would continue narrowing her life around it.
